info.bio:
The Clash fue una banda londinense de punk rock que estuvo activa entre el año1976 hasta el 1986. El grupo fue uno de los más importantes e icónicos de la primera ola del punk, originada a fines de los años '70 y, a diferencia de la mayoría de las bandas punk que se caracterizaban por su simplicidad musical, ellos incorporaron Rock and Roll, Reggae, Rockabilly, y puntualmente otros estilos en su repertorio. 


Sumado a esto, The Clash también exhibió una intencionalidad política en sus letras que con el tiempo se convertiría en su característica distintiva fundamental. La pasión y el idealismo expresado en las composiciones de Joe Strummer y Mick Jones, contrastó con el nihilismo de los Sex Pistols y la sencillez de Ramones, las otras bandas emblemas del punk en la época. Su álbum de 1979, London Calling, es considerado uno de los mejores discos de la historia del Rock & Roll. 

La actitud, el estilo y la originalidad lírica de The Clash han tenido una gran influencia en un sinnúmero de artistas, tanto dentro como fuera de la escena punk. A lo largo del tiempo, se ha acuñado entre los fanáticos y los críticos un apodo atribuido en una ocasión por su discográfica CBS Records: "La Única Banda Que Importa" -"The Only Band That Matters"-. El uso del mismo indica, entre otras lecturas, el compromiso que el grupo asumió al nunca desviarse de sus ideales para buscar beneficios económicos. En el año 2003 fueron incluidos en el Salón de la Fama del Rock & Roll.

scenes.name: Punk rock (1976-77)
scenes.book: Postpunk. Romper todo y empezar de nuevo
scenes.author: Simon Reynolds
scenes.desc: El «Año Cero»: hacia el verano de 1977 el punk ya era una parodia de sí mismo y su frágil alianza entre chicos obreros y bohemios de escuela de arte se rompe. De un lado quedan los «punks verdaderos», populistas, que desembocarán en el Oi! y el hardcore; del otro, la vanguardia que se llamará postpunk, que vio en 1977 no un retorno al rock crudo sino la ocasión de romper con la tradición. Su legado común: la fe en el poder de la música y el «hazlo tú mismo».

scenes.name: Punk-rock británico
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: La gira de los Ramones de 1976 contagia a Inglaterra, donde el punk es combinación de moda y paro: la Gran Bretaña de Thatcher, con las ciudades industriales devastadas, convierte el «punk» en algo mucho más serio que lo que pretendían los Ramones. Malcolm McLaren inventa el sonido (Sex Pistols, «los Ramones con heroína y valium») y la imagen. The Clash, los más intelectuales (London Calling, Sandinista); Damned, Generation X, Buzzcocks (inventores del punk-pop), Vibrators. En Australia, Radio Birdman y los Saints. La segunda ola (GBH, UK Subs, Neurotics, New Model Army, Stiff Little Fingers) y el punk anarquista (Crass, Discharge, Rudimentari Peni, Subhumans).

podcast.title: Impact on UK Music Scene (1975)
podcast.body: The Clash were identified as one of three bands, alongside The Sex Pistols and The Saints, that "changed the music forever in the UK," following the media frenzy over The Saints' 1976 single. Their emergence in England coincided with the germination of punk rock in New York by 1975. "Because of that media freak out, three bands changed the music forever in the UK, the sex pistols, the clash, and the Saints."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: 100 Club Punk Rock Festival Performance (September 20, 1976)
podcast.body: The Clash performed at Britain's first official punk rock festival held at the 100 Club on Oxford Street, London. This festival, alongside the Sex Pistols and The Damned, marked a turning point where punk rock became widely known. "This was the site of Britain's first official punk rock festival."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Part of British Punk Rock Explosion (Summer 1976)
podcast.body: The Clash's ascent coincided with the "British punk rock explosion," which ignited in the summer of 1976. Alongside the Sex Pistols and other bands, they were central to this movement, leading to the adoption of the term "punk rock" from New York to christen this new British musical phenomenon. "This coincided with the rise of the sex pistols and the clash in all the other groups who were really part of the British punk rock explosion which began in the summer of 1976."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Witnessing The Ramones (July 4, 1976)
podcast.body: Members of the newly formed Clash, including Joe Strummer, were present at The Ramones' July 4, 1976 gig at the Roundhouse in London. Strummer recounted how they got backstage by forming a "human chain" through a window to meet The Ramones, describing it as a "really great punk rock moment." "Members of the newly formed clash, Chrissy Hind of the still unformed pretenders, the damn who would become the first British punk band to release a record, Generation X featuring a very young Billy Isle. They were all at these gigs and they were all transformed by what they saw and heard."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Arrested for Stealing a Pillowcase and Towels – Newcastle, June 1977, Fined 100 Pounds
podcast.body: On June 11, 1977, Joe Strummer and Topper Headon were in Newcastle. The following night they were arrested on robbery charges for allegedly stealing a pillowcase and several towels from a Holiday Inn. They were supposed to have appeared in court in May 1977 to answer these charges but had simply not turned up. A judge took a dim view of the non-appearance; in the end they were fined 100 pounds each. "I mean, the Clash. They were arrested for stealing a pillowcase."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: CBS Records Contract (1977)
podcast.body: On January 25, 1977, The Clash signed a worldwide recording contract with CBS Records for 100,000 pounds. This occurred at the height of punk rock in the UK. The deal sparked outrage among other punk bands and fans, who viewed it as a betrayal of their anti-capitalist, populist punk rebel image. The fanzine Stephen Glue even declared "punk died the day the clash signed to CBS." "And on January 25, 1977, at the very height of punk rock in the UK, they signed a worldwide recording contract with CBS records for 100,000 pounds."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Controversial Major Label Signing (1977)
podcast.body: On January 26, 1977, The Clash signed a significant record deal with CBS, a major multinational corporation. This deal, valued at 100,000 pounds (reportedly 75,000 pounds higher than competing offers), sparked outrage and accusations of "sell out" from their fans across the UK. Despite being perceived as uncompromisingly socialist and anti-establishment, the band maintained they aimed to "corrupt the music industry from within." "The day the clash allegedly sold out January 26, 1977."

podcast.title: Mick Jones in Sid Vicious's New York Band – September 1978
podcast.body: Mick Jones, guitarist for The Clash, joined Sid Vicious's temporary band for three shows at Max's Kansas City in New York in September 1978. "He had a band together, consisting of two guys from the New York Dolls and Mick Jones of the Clash."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Poor Record Deal and Management Change (1978)
podcast.body: Bernie Rhodes negotiated a "very poor record deal" for The Clash, which led the band to turn against him. Consequently, Rhodes was out as their manager in 1978 and was replaced by Carolyn Coon, a painter and rock journalist.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Hepatitis from Gobbing – 1979, Spat in Mouth During Performance
podcast.body: In the early British punk scene, audience members competed to spit at bands on stage as a sign of enthusiasm following a newspaper article depicting the practice. During a 1979 Clash performance, Joe Strummer was singing with his mouth open when an audience member's spit landed directly in it. The result was a significant case of hepatitis. The practice of spitting at performers, known as "gobbing," was common enough that performers were routinely covered in phlegm and mucus during shows. "Joe Strummer was singing. His mouth was open and the result was a really nasty case of hepatitis."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Paul Simonon's Bass Trashing Incident (1979)
podcast.body: During a show at the Palladium in New York on September 21, 1979, bassist Paul Simonon smashed his instrument on stage. His frustration stemmed from the crowd's perceived lack of engagement, which he attributed to bouncers preventing the audience from standing up. The incident occurred around 10:43 pm, as evidenced by his broken wristwatch. This moment was captured in an iconic, out-of-focus photograph by Penny Smith, which later became the cover of "London Calling." "Simmon was in a very bad mood that night at the palladium in New York. He was upset that the crowd just wasn't into the gig, largely because the bouncers had refused to let the audience stand up and get into the show."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Bernie Rhodes' Re-hiring and Internal Strife (1981)
podcast.body: Rhodes was re-hired in 1981 after the band was unsuccessfully managed by Joe Strummer's girlfriend. Upon his return, he actively worked to pit Joe Strummer and Mick Jones against each other, possibly with the goal of becoming the band's musical director. "But then he was re-hired in 1981 after the group was unsuccessfully run by Joe Stromer's girlfriend. And this is where things went wrong again."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Creative Control Conflict (1981)
podcast.body: During the recording of *Rat Patrol from Fort Bragg* in 1981, founding member Mick Jones and Joe Strummer were in conflict over creative control. Jones, along with drummer Topper Heaton, was exploring Dub, Reggae, and world music, leading to longer songs, while Strummer disliked this direction and desired a concise, single album due to the band's debt with CBS. This led to them working in separate studios. "At the time, Mick Jones, the founder of the group, was fighting with Joe Strummer over creative control... it got to the point where Mick was working on material in one studio, and Joe was working on his clash material in another."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Debt with Label (1981)
podcast.body: The Clash had gone "deep into debt" with their label, CBS, which influenced Joe Strummer's desire for a "nice tight single album" for effective promotion, contrasting with Mick Jones's more sprawling vision for *Rat Patrol from Fort Bragg*. "after going deep into debt with their label, Joe wanted a nice tight single album that CBS could promote effectively."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Re-engagement and Musical Influence (1981)
podcast.body: After Carolyn Coon's management didn't work out, and neither did the company that followed, Bernie Rhodes was back managing The Clash in 1981, while also managing other bands like Dexys Midnight Runners. During this period, Rhodes notably convinced the band that 12-inch dance remixes were a beneficial idea, which led to the creation of the dance mix for "The Magnificent Seven."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Joe Strummer's Disappearance (1982)
podcast.body: Joe Strummer, a key voice of the British punk explosion, inexplicably vanished on April 26, 1982, the night before The Clash was due to leave on a major tour, forcing the tour to be scrapped. He was gone for eight full weeks, showing up suddenly in mid-May 1982, offering various unconfirmed explanations like running the Paris marathon or helping a girlfriend's mother out of jail, leading to speculation about a publicity stunt or burnout; this vanishing act retrospectively marked the beginning of the end for the band. "Joe Strummer, one of the voices of the whole British punk explosion had inexplicably disappeared, vanished."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 2

podcast.title: Joe Strummer's Disappearance (March-May 1982)
podcast.body: In March 1982, Joe Strummer suddenly disappeared for eight weeks after a phone interview with a journalist, leading to a tour cancellation and uncertainty about his well-being. This event occurred just before the release of *Combat Rock*. It was later rumored to be a publicity stunt orchestrated by the band's manager, with Joe reportedly spending his time in France to help a girlfriend bail her mother out of jail.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Possible Influence from Rashid Taha (1982)
podcast.body: After a 1982 show in Paris, Algerian singer-songwriter Rashid Taha, leader of the French Arab-punk band Residence Permit, gave Joe Strummer a demo cassette. A year later, Taha noted stylistic similarities between his demo and "Rock the Casbah," leading to speculation about whether The Clash drew inspiration from his material, though Taha never expressed bitterness and even covered the song himself. "Was Rock the Casbah inspired by what was handed to Joe on that sidewalk that night? Maybe."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Topper Headon's Dismissal (May 10, 1982)
podcast.body: Drummer Topper Headon was let go on May 10, 1982, due to his "monstrous heroin habit." "First it was Jermore Topper Heaton, who had a monstrous heroin habit. He was let go on May 10th, 1982."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Firing of Mick Jones (September 1, 1983) – Manager-Engineered Split That Destroyed the Band
podcast.body: Manager Bernie Rhodes had spent years pitting Joe Strummer against Mick Jones, encouraging Joe to fire him. On September 1, 1983, Mick Jones's departure was announced in a formal "Clash Communiqué" stating he had "drifted apart from the original idea of the Clash." The resulting lineup recorded the critically panned *Cut the Crap* (1985), featuring two new members, after which the Clash simply dissolved with no official announcement. Mick Jones went on to major success with Big Audio Dynamite, while Strummer spent over a decade in record-company limbo and never again achieved the stature he had with the Clash. "Firing Mick Jones? Terrible. Joe Strummer thought he knew better than Mick, and he ended up paying for it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Mick Jones' Dismissal (September 1, 1983)
podcast.body: Guitarist Mick Jones was fired on September 1, 1983, a decision announced via a "clash communique" that stated he had "drifted apart from the original idea of the clash." This followed increasing difficulties, including being late for rehearsals and recording, refusing tours, and his relationship with Joe Strummer deteriorating due to Bernie Rhodes's machinations. Joe Strummer expressed frustration about having to "beg him to play the guitar," comparing the situation to "dragging a dead dog around." "It was September 1st, 1983, and his firing was announced in what was called a clash communique."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Mick Jones's Firing (September 1983)
podcast.body: In September 1983, Joe Strummer orchestrated what was described as a "coup" by issuing an "infamous clash communique," essentially firing Mick Jones, who had co-founded The Clash in 1976. Joe expressed frustration with Mick's perceived lack of commitment, stating he had to "beg him to play the guitar" and comparing the situation to "dragging a dead dog around on a bit of string." This decision was widely seen as detrimental, and The Clash "was never the same after Mick left."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Reformation Proposal (1990)
podcast.body: Mick Jones proposed reforming The Clash around 1990. However, Joe Strummer's insistence on the original late 70s/early 80s lineup (Joe, Mick, Paul Simonon, Topper Headon or Terry Chimes) and their former manager Bernie Rhodes (who had tried to sue them) led to the other members refusing the plan, and the reformation never occurred. "Mick Jones came calling, suggesting that he and Joe reform the clash."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Joe Strummer's Death (December 2002)
podcast.body: Joe Strummer of The Clash died just before Christmas in 2002 from a heart attack. "Joe Strummer of the Clash, heart attack just before Christmas, 2002."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Joe Strummer's Death (December 22, 2002)
podcast.body: Joe Strummer passed away from a heart attack on December 22, 2002. His death received some newspaper coverage in the last weeks of 2002, but the narrative suggests this coverage "didn't even come close to doing the man justice."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Mick Jones's Production for The Libertines (2002)
podcast.body: Mick Jones, guitarist for The Clash, produced The Libertines' 2002 album, referred to in the transcript as "Liberty and Stabby Welvent." This collaboration is highlighted in a segment discussing Pete Doherty. "which was produced by Mick Jones of the Clash."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Rock and Roll Hall of Fame Induction (March 10, 2003)
podcast.body: The Rock and Roll Hall of Fame induction ceremony in New York on March 10, 2003, presented "the best ever prospect for a clash reunion." There were strong indications that the band would reunite to play up to three songs for the occasion, but Joe Strummer's death in December 2002 prevented his attendance. "Their induction ceremony into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in New York on March 10th, 2003."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: "London Calling" Recognition
podcast.body: During an impromptu street performance by Joe Strummer in Toronto, a passerby remarked on his talent and compared his sound to "a lot" and then specifically "that guy was that London calling," indicating the iconic status and recognition of the song. "That guy was that London calling."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: "No Beatles, Elvis, or Rolling Stones" Slogan
podcast.body: Since 1977, The Clash had adopted the slogan "No Beatles, Elvis, or Rolling Stones" to assert their unique identity and reject the rock establishment. This stance created significant controversy and confusion among their fans when they decided to go on a big stadium and arena tour with The Who in September 1982.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: "Rock the Casbah" Lyric Reference
podcast.body: The Clash's song "Rock the Casbah" contains a line that references Bernie Rhodes, specifically Joe Strummer singing: "now the king told his boogeyman, you have to let that ragged drop." This lyric is interpreted as Strummer referring to a situation where the record company insisted on dropping the eight-minute song "Sean Flynn" from the *Combat Rock* album, and Bernie Rhodes was the one who agreed to its removal.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Activism and Affordability for Fans
podcast.body: The Clash consistently prioritized their fans and their anti-capitalist ideals. They insisted that the price of their albums and concert tickets be substantially lower than prevailing rates. The band members also maintained a salary of only $200 a week per man, even after achieving world fame with *London Calling*, to reflect their understanding of scraping by. They would often open back doors at concerts to let in fans who couldn't afford tickets, meet audiences for beers after shows, and once donated a limousine sent by their record company to a committee for striking Welsh miners.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Alleged KGB Financing of Punk
podcast.body: An alleged retired KGB agent, Alexander Vaternukhov Volition, falsely claimed that the entire punk movement, including The Clash, The Sex Pistols, and The Ramones, was financed by the Soviet secret police to "create utter chaos" and promote "nihilist, anti-establishment and anti-American ideologies." This story, originating from a satirical news site, is entirely fake. "He claims that the entire punk movement from the sex pistols to the clash to the Ramones was financed by the Soviet secret police."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Great KGB Punk Rock Conspiracy

podcast.title: Alt-Rock Pioneer Recognition
podcast.body: In the early 1990s, The Clash were recognized as alt-rock pioneers, mentioned alongside Iggy Pop, The Velvet Underground, The Ramones, and The Sex Pistols for their foundational influence on the genre. "Iggy was once again named as a legendary alt-rock pioneer right out there with a velvet underground on the rambones and the sex pistols and the clash."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About Iggy Pop

podcast.title: Anti-Establishment Stance
podcast.body: The Clash were known for their strong anti-establishment stance, actively "sticking it to the establishment, kicking against the class system and railing against the status quo." Their politically charged music resonated with anti-capitalist sentiments and paralleled the aims of certain leftist and nationalist organizations that the KGB might have sought to encourage. "Things like the sex festivals and the clash were all about sticking it to the establishment, kicking against the class system and railing against the status quo."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Band Lifespan Template Adherence
podcast.body: The Clash is cited as a band that closely followed Don Letts' theory on the average useful lifespan of a band, which typically involves a period of intense activity, a peak around year four or five, and then an inevitable decline due to internal and external conflicts. "Now the clash certainly followed that template, sort of the Beatles and the Smiths."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Sloan In Their Own Words: Part 1

podcast.title: Band Lifespan and Best Work
podcast.body: Don Letz, a DJ, filmmaker, and confidant of The Clash, observed that the average lifespan of a band is seven years, typically sufficient for them to form, become famous, develop creative differences, and break up. The Clash's most impactful work occurred between 1976 and 1983, fitting this observation. "The average lifespan of a band is seven years."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall and Rise of Blink 182 Part 3

podcast.title: Band's "Ridiculous Pains" Philosophy
podcast.body: An unnamed member of The Clash expressed pride in the band's "ridiculous pains," suggesting a deliberate and challenging approach to their art that they were committed to maintaining.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 9

podcast.title: Band's Demise from Internal Politics
podcast.body: The Clash ultimately imploded due to internal politics, with their true demise occurring after Joe Strummer fired Mick Jones, a co-founder of the band. "The clash, a band that was eventually torn apart by internal politics, but their real demise came after Joe Strummer fired Mick Jones."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Bernie Rhodes' Initial Firing (After Second Album)
podcast.body: Bernie Rhodes, credited with mentoring The Clash through their early years, was fired after their second album. While cited as "creative differences," the actual reason was his poor management, including negotiating a highly unfavorable 13-album deal with CBS and causing the band to fall deeply into debt. "The first person to get the axe was manager Bernie Rhodes... A big part of the reason Bernie was axed was because under his supervision, the band fell deeply into debt."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Bootlegs of Rat Patrol from Fort Bragg
podcast.body: Although *Rat Patrol from Fort Bragg* was never officially released, bootleg versions of the album exist, allowing fans to hear the original material. "But what of Rat Patrol from Fort Bragg? Well, bootlegs exist. And I just happened to have one."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Box Set Collection
podcast.body: A couple of box sets from The Clash are mentioned as being in a collection, highlighting their legacy and the market for their comprehensive releases. "Couple From The Clash."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: British Punk Standard - 1970s
podcast.body: The Clash represented the British spin on punk rock in the 1970s, establishing a significant movement within the UK music scene. "In the 1970s, it was the British spin on punk rock with the pistols and the clash."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt Rock: Chapter 12

podcast.title: British Rock Tradition
podcast.body: The Clash was mentioned as part of the proud tradition of British rock and roll that needed to be saved from the "grunge marauders" invading from the US. "Her majesty's empire needed to be saved from the grunge marauders, the proud tradition of British rock and roll, the Beatles, the Stones, Led Zeppelin, Sexbistles, Clash, Bowie, it all needed to be saved from the likes of Nirvana and Pearl Jam and Soundgarden."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Broad Range of Protest Themes
podcast.body: The Clash distinguished themselves by not only railing against typical establishment targets but also by wading into a wide array of other complex issues. Their lyrics tackled imperialism (both political and cultural), police brutality, unethical corporate behavior, crime, terrorism, rioting, immigration, and racism, establishing them as a band with something to say about virtually everything. "Take the clash, for example, while they railed against the usual suspects they waited into other choppy waters, imperialism, political and cultural, police brutality, bad corporate behavior, crime, terrorism, rioting, immigration, racism."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Camden Rehearsal Space
podcast.body: The band rehearsed in a building in Camden, which notably featured a jukebox. This jukebox was stocked with the latest singles from contemporary bands like The Ramones, as well as reggae songs from Jamaican artists such as Bob Marley and dub pioneer Lee Scratch Perry. The Clash particularly favored Dub music, identifying it as the music of the immigrant communities with whom they shared their neighborhood. "The clash rehearsed in a building in Camden that featured a jukebox stock with the latest singles from bands like The Ramones and Reggae Songs from Jamaican artists like Bob Marley and Dub Pioneer Lee Scratch Perry."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Chiropractic Clinic in Essex
podcast.body: Today, Terry Chimes runs his own chiropractic clinic located in Essex. "And today, Terry Chimes has a chiropractic clinic in Essex."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Chrissie Hynde's Early Involvement
podcast.body: Chrissie Hynde played guitar in an early punk band that eventually morphed into The Clash, highlighting her deep roots in the formative punk scene. "She played guitar in some early punk bands, including one that eventually morphed into the clash..."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Post-Punk Explosion Part 1: New Wave

podcast.title: Contemporaries of The Slits
podcast.body: The Clash were contemporaries of The Slits, an all-female English punk band that served as an inspiration for the Riot Grrrl movement. They were part of the same original punk rock scene in England. "who were contemporaries of the sex pistols in the clash."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Contrast to No Wave
podcast.body: The Clash is cited as a point of comparison, highlighting how different the No Wave scene was in its musical approach during the late 1970s. "This was not Van Halen or even the clash."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Cultural Icon of Political Punk
podcast.body: The Clash, particularly through Joe Strummer, were regarded as the quintessential political and activist punk band, embodying a defiant spirit that resonated with millions worldwide and refused to compromise. "He was the political punk, the activist punk, the punk that refused to bend. For millions around the world, he was the guy who embodied the best of the punk spirit."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 100 Greatest Rock Moments of the Millennium So Far - Part 8: (30-21)

podcast.title: Daughter's Crafting and Gardening Skills
podcast.body: Joe Strummer's daughter, Jazz Domino Holly, is noted for her craftiness. She is a knitter, makes duvets, cooks, and is an avid gardener. She even authored a handbook covering these subjects. "she makes duvetes, cooks, and is an avid gardener."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Debunked KGB Financing Allegation
podcast.body: A false story, originating from a satirical website, claimed that the entire punk movement, including The Clash, was financed by the Soviet secret police. This fabrication suggested the KGB aimed to create chaos and promote nihilist, anti-establishment, and anti-American ideologies in the West. "He claims that the entire punk movement from the sex pistols to the clash to the Ramones was financed by the Soviet secret police."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Definition of Punk
podcast.body: The Clash is identified as a definitive punk band, characterized by their enthusiastic and angry guitar thrashing and three-chord fast-paced style, placed in the same category as the Sex Pistols and Ramones. "For example, the sex pistols in the clash, Ramones definitely punk."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Don Letts' Theory Connection
podcast.body: Don Letts, a British DJ and filmmaker close to The Clash during the original punk scene, developed a theory that the optimal lifespan for most bands is seven to nine years. He suggests that this period allows for birth, rise, peak, and then explosion due to internal pressures like creative differences. The Clash are cited as an example of a brilliant band for their time that, despite multi-million dollar offers, never reunited to record new material. "He was especially close with the clash. And he has a theory. He believes the average and proper lifespan of most bands is seven years, nine at the outside."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Arrests and Fines
podcast.body: The Clash gained a reputation as "criminals" due to frequent incidents. On June 10, 1977, Joe Strummer and Topper Headon were arrested for spray-painting "the clash" on a wall. They were later fined 100 pounds for stealing a pillowcase from a Holiday Inn, and 800 pounds for shooting at expensive racing pigeons. Mick Jones also faced trouble for cocaine possession.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Inspiration – London Punk Years
podcast.body: In late 1976 and through 1977, The Clash drew heavy inspiration from the social and economic turmoil in London during the punk rock era. The English economy was in shambles with strikes, high unemployment, rolling blackouts, and a pervasive class system. The band sought to document the experiences of being young, poor, and desperate in Britain during this period. "Inspiration was taken from what they saw around them in London during the punk years."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Political and Social Awareness
podcast.body: The Clash were distinguished from their punk contemporaries like the Sex Pistols and Ramones by their militant, passionate, and serious political and social awareness. They believed their agenda could change the world, aiming to change the system and rock and roll from the ground up, even if their expectations sometimes clashed with reality.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Punk and Dub Experimentation
podcast.body: The Clash initially began as a "two chord" punk band but later ventured into experimenting with dub music, showcasing how early punk allowed for diverse sounds. "The clash started out as two chord wonders, but then started experimenting with dub."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: East German Stasi Opposition
podcast.body: The Clash desired to bring their music to audiences in communist East Germany, believing their working-class, socialist, and anti-capitalist message would be well-received. However, the East German secret police, the Stasi, had been monitoring The Clash and studying Joe Strummer's lyrics. They concluded that the band was "just a little too left wing and a little too incendiary" to be allowed into the country, denying them visas.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Enhanced Message through Musical Fusion
podcast.body: The Clash believed that by throwing away old punk dogmas and injecting new musical ideas, they could make their socially conscious messages about racism, drug abuse, corrupt cops, and unemployment even more potent and impactful. "So the clash thought, look, we can do anything. We can throw away the old punk dogmas, inject them with these new ideas, and this will just make our messages about racism and drug abuse and corrupt cops and unemployment even more powerful."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Ethos and Contradictions
podcast.body: Joe Strummer and The Clash were characterized as idealistic, conflicted, and confused, embodying both reactionary and revolutionary tendencies. They championed the working class and the poor, and "sneered at consumerism and the privileged," yet controversially sold their songs for TV commercials, advertising products like Levi's jeans and Jaguar cars. "They championed the working class and the poor and sneered at consumerism and the privileged yet they had no trouble selling their songs to TV commercials to advertise things like Levi's jeans and Jaguar cars."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Evolution from Chrissie Hynde's Band
podcast.body: One of the short-lived British punk bands in which Chrissie Hynde played guitar during her early days in London later evolved into The Clash, establishing a direct link between her punk roots and the formation of this major punk act. "She also played guitar in several short-lived British punk bands, one of which later revolved into the clash."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Evolution from London SS
podcast.body: The Clash evolved out of a prominent British punk band known as the London SS, which was famous for never playing a gig. Many musicians passed through London SS, including Chrissie Hynde, who later formed The Pretenders. "The Clash evolved out of the most famous British punk band to never play a gig. They were called the London SS."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Forced Studio Change
podcast.body: The Clash were compelled to leave The Power Station studio when their recording budget ran out, leading them to relocate their sessions to Electric Lady Studios. "The clash had been working at another studio called the Power Station, but the clash were kicked out when the money ran out."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Formation Date and Naming
podcast.body: The closest estimate for The Clash's formation date is June 6, 1976. During rehearsals, the group considered various names such as The Mirrors, The Outsiders, The Psychotic Negatives, The Phones, The Heart Drops, and The Weak Heart Drops. The name "Clash" was ultimately chosen after the bass player read a newspaper headline describing a "Clash with police." "The closest we can come down to nailing a date for the Clash's formation is June 6th, 1976."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Formation History
podcast.body: Joe, the guitarist for The 101ers, was profoundly influenced by the Sex Pistols' attitude and energy when they opened for his band at the Nashville club, despite their "awful" musicianship. A few days later, Joe left The 101ers and began forming a new band with others who admired the Sex Pistols. This new group went through several name changes—The Psychotic Negatives, The Weak Heart Drops, The Outsiders, The Mirrors in the Evening Standards—before finally settling on The Clash. "It was their attitude and their energy that grabbed his attention."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Very First Episode of the Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Formation Relative to Devo
podcast.body: The Clash started playing approximately four years after Devo formed in Akron, Ohio. "about four years before the clash."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Formation and Early Mentorship
podcast.body: Bernie Rhodes, after being rebuffed in his offer to co-manage the Sex Pistols, sought to create his own version of the band and found The Clash. Initially, their relationship was positive, with Rhodes mentoring the group and convincing them to write about contemporary social and political issues.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Garage Rock Core
podcast.body: The Clash are described as having a Garage Rock core because of their "back to basics approach," aligning them with the fundamental spirit of the genre despite their punk rock context. "The sex pistols, the clash, the damned, all those groups are garage rock bands at their core because of their back to basics approach."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alt Rock Revivals Part 4: Garage Rock

podcast.title: Genre Ambiguity in Late 70s/Early 80s
podcast.body: Towards the late 1970s and early 1980s, the evolution of The Clash led to confusion and questions about their evolving musical direction. This implied they were exploring new subgenres beyond strict punk, such as Techno-pop, Goth, or Ska. "What the hell is going on with a clash?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Iconic Album Cover Image
podcast.body: The cover of *London Calling* features Paul Simmonon smashing his bass, which is described as one of the most iconic rock photos ever. "And by the way, that's him smashing his bass on the cover of London Calling."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Influence on Grunge Bands
podcast.body: The Clash was listed as an influence on grunge musicians, demonstrating that while 90s bands embraced older metal, they also maintained their connection to punk roots. "Yeah, we were into the clash and black flag and the replacements in the Dead Kennedys 2."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Influence on Hardcore
podcast.body: The Clash were noted as an influence on the punk rock styles from which early hardcore music drew inspiration. "The punk rock styles, the sex pistols, the romones, and the clash were influenced, but so was the heavy metal of the era."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Influence on Living Color
podcast.body: The Clash was one of the key inspirations for Living Color, influencing their unique funk metal sound. "They were inspired equally by James Brown, Funkadelic, Run DMC, Slion the Family Stone, and Led Zeppelin Van Halen, and the Clash."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Influence on Oasis's Sound
podcast.body: Oasis's guitar pop was noted for being as loud as anything The Clash had done, but with more groove and melody, showing their influence on the intensity of later bands. "This was guitar pop as loud as anything the sex pistols or the clash had done, but with much more of a groove and with more melody."

podcast.title: Influence on Punk Rock
podcast.body: The Clash's "energy and the vision" and the "risks they took" are credited with preventing punk from fizzling out completely at the end of the 1970s. The band is considered foundational for "three-cord, punk-inspired rock and everything that came after." "punk may have fizzled out completely at the end of the 1970s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Influence on The Black Keys
podcast.body: The Clash were among the favorite bands that inspired the short hooks for the songs composed on The Black Keys' *El Camino* album, showcasing the punk influences on their sound. "and the Clash".

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Influences and Recording of London Calling
podcast.body: The Clash's "London Calling" was a product of various influences and circumstances, including their North American tour which provided new ideas, their frustration with management and label, and the socio-political climate of Britain's "Winter of Discontent," a period of massive strikes. Recognizing that punk was evolving, the band moved forward by incorporating diverse musical styles. The album, containing 19 songs, was recorded with remarkable speed, with 12 tracks finished in just three days in August 1979, showcasing the band's immense energy. "The clash had so many new ideas and so many new songs and so much energy that this album was recorded in just a few days."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Inspiration from London's Troubles
podcast.body: In the late 1970s, particularly 1976 and 1977, The Clash drew inspiration from the dire conditions in London, which included an economy in shambles, widespread strikes, high unemployment, rolling blackouts, and the crushing British class system. The band sought to document the experience of being young, poor, and desperate in Britain during this period. "Inspiration was taken from what they saw around them in London during the punk years."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Interviewed by Host
podcast.body: The Clash were among the artists interviewed by the host over the years. "I've had the privilege of talking to a ton of really cool people over the years...The Clash."

podcast.title: Jigsaw Puzzles as Merchandise
podcast.body: In 2020, The Clash offered jigsaw puzzles as part of their new merchandise range, an example of artists exploring alternative revenue streams. "Jigsaw puzzles from the Clash ACDC and Nirvana, among others."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Joe Strummer Adopts Mohawk After Taxi Driver
podcast.body: Joe Strummer of The Clash was inspired by Robert De Niro's Mohawk in the 1976 movie "Taxi Driver" and subsequently shaved his own head into the style, initiating a trend for punks and their admirers to emulate and develop. "So Joe shaved his head in a Mohawk, thereby sitting up a trend for all punks and punk admirers to copy and evolve."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Joe Strummer's Acting and Composing Career
podcast.body: Following his work on the *Sid and Nancy* soundtrack, Joe Strummer found an unexpected calling in film. He developed a good relationship with director Alex Cox, leading to acting roles in Cox's next two movies. In the 1987 film *Walker*, set in 19th-century Nicaragua, Joe played a character named Fossett and composed all the music for the soundtrack. The same year, he appeared in another Alex Cox movie, *Straight to Hell*, a surreal western, playing a character named Sims. He continued doing movie work, both acting and composing, for the rest of the 1980s, including the soundtracks for *Permanent Record* (1988) and *Mystery Train* (1989).

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Joe Strummer's Background
podcast.body: The last member to join the group was Joe Strummer, whose real name was John Millers. He was a "refugee" from a pub rock band called The 101ers and insisted on being addressed by his new moniker. Millers, the son of an international diplomat, had a somewhat "posh" upbringing but intentionally abandoned it to become a busker. He earned the name "Strummer" due to the intense ferocity with which he played his guitar. "The last member of the group to join was a refugee from a pub rock band called the 101ers, and he insisted on being addressed as Joe Strummer."

podcast.title: Joe Strummer's Cause of Death
podcast.body: Joe Strummer died on December 22nd, 2002, from an intra-mural coronary artery, a rare genetic condition where a main blood vessel of the heart grows within the muscle wall, eventually squeezing shut and causing a fatal heart attack. "The cause of death was an intra-mural coronary artery."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Joe Strummer's Last Performance
podcast.body: Joe Strummer's final performance occurred on November 24th, 2002, with his band The Mescaleros at Liverpool University, just one month before his sudden passing. "On November 24th, 2002, John is banned the Mescalero's play to show at Liverpool University."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Joe Strummer's London Marathon
podcast.body: While the myth of Joe Strummer running a Paris marathon in a chicken suit is false, he did genuinely run the London marathon. His official time was four hours and forty-three minutes, and he accomplished this impressive feat without any proper training. "Joe most certainly ran the London marathon and his official time was four hours and forty three minutes and that he did it without any proper training."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Joe Strummer's Marathon Myth
podcast.body: Manager Bernie Rhodes created a false story in 1982 that Joe Strummer had disappeared and his safety was feared, ahead of the "Combat Rock" album release. Joe genuinely took a vacation to Paris, where he reportedly ran a local marathon, with varying times of "four hours and thirty minutes" or "three hours and twenty minutes" reported, and claims of drinking ten pints of beer the night before. This story mutated into the myth that he ran a marathon in Paris dressed in a chicken suit, which is untrue, though he did run the London marathon in four hours and forty-three minutes without proper training. "Somehow this mutated into the story of Joe running the marathon in disguise and eventually that disguise became a chicken suit. Sorry to say, but it's not true."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Joe Strummer's Rap Influence
podcast.body: During the period between studio sessions, Joe Strummer spent time exploring New York City, where he became acquainted with and influenced by early rap sounds, particularly Grandmaster Flash, which then permeated into their song "The Magnificent Seven." "Joe Strummer had plenty of time to wander New York where he started to pick up on the sound to rap. Grandmaster Flash became a favorite. And this song definitely features those early rap influences."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Joe Strummer's Sudden Passing
podcast.body: Joe Strummer died quickly and without drama; he went for a dog walk, returned home, passed through the kitchen, and then sat on the sofa where he passed away. "Joe's death was quick and without any drama. He went out to walk the dog, came home, went through the kitchen, sat on the sofa, and that was it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Joe Strummer's Unexpected Death
podcast.body: Joe Strummer's death came as a complete surprise, given his lifestyle that included running marathons and being a vegetarian since 1971, despite being a smoker and enjoying a drink. "No one saw this coming. Yes, he was a smoker. Yes, he enjoyed a drink. But he also ran marathons."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Joe Strummer's Work with Big Audio Dynamite
podcast.body: Despite the acrimony of their split, Joe Strummer and Mick Jones maintained their songwriting partnership. In 1986, two weeks before the movie *Sid and Nancy* was released, Mick Jones's band, Big Audio Dynamite, released their second album, *Number 10 Upping Street*. Eight of the 12 songs on this album featured contributions from Joe Strummer.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Lifelong "Ticking Time Bomb"
podcast.body: Joe Strummer lived his entire life with this undetected genetic condition, which acted as a "ticking time bomb" in his chest, capable of causing sudden death at any moment. "For his entire life, Joe had this ticking time bomb in his chest that could have gone off at any moment."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Lollapalooza Reunion Attempt (Mid-1990s)
podcast.body: In the mid-1990s, rumors circulated about a potential Clash reunion for the Lollapalooza Festival. Organizers reportedly offered the band an open price to reunite, and sources suggested they were "really really close" to a deal, even beginning casting for a potential Clash video, though it ultimately never materialized. "One source told me that they were so close to a deal that they had already started casting people for some kind of clash video."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: London Calling Album Artwork
podcast.body: The iconic artwork for "London Calling" features a black and white photograph with green and pink lettering, a color scheme that serves as a tribute to an old Elvis Presley record. The cover also famously depicts bassist Paul Simonon smashing his bass guitar, a moment captured at 10:50 PM on September 21, 1979, at the Palladium in New York City. This precise time is known because Paul's watch broke and stopped at the exact moment he destroyed his instrument. "First the color scheme, the black and white photo and the green and pink lettering. That's actually a tribute to an old Elvis Presley record."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Major Label Punk
podcast.body: The Clash were referenced as a punk band that had signed with a major label, supporting the argument that collaborating with the mainstream could be seen as a form of "subverting the system from within," thus maintaining punk or alternative credentials. "And weren't the Ramones and the Sex Pistols and the Clash all in major labels?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Manager Bernie Rhodes
podcast.body: Bernie Rhodes was The Clash's manager during their early days but was later fired. After his dismissal, he notably attempted to sue the band, creating a significant rift that prevented him from being part of any potential reunion plans. "But most crucially, the reformed clash would have to be managed by Bernie Rhodes, their manager from the old days."

podcast.body: Mick Gallagher, known for his work with The Animals and Ian Dury and the Blockheads, also contributed keyboards to several tracks by The Clash. "as well as playing on several tracks by the clash."

podcast.body: On "one or two occasions," Mick Jones of The Clash joined Sid Vicious's solo band during his attempt to launch a solo career in New York. "On one or two occasions, the group also featured Mick Jones of the clash."

podcast.title: Mohawk Popularized in Music by Joe Strummer
podcast.body: While the Mohawk's origins are linked to a Robert De Niro film, Joe Strummer of The Clash is widely recognized as the individual who popularized the haircut within the music industry. "The clash featuring Joe Strummer, the popularizer of the Mohawk haircut in music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Motivated by New York Scene
podcast.body: By April 1976, when the Ramones' debut album was released, The Clash were formed but had "barely played a note together." They, along with other nascent British punk bands, were motivated by reports of what was happening in New York and were eager to see the Ramones. "The clash were together, but they'd barely played a note together."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Musical Expansion of Punk Rock
podcast.body: The Clash were instrumental in enlarging the musical scope of punk rock, insisting that diverse genres like rockabilly and reggae could also be considered punk. Joe Strummer, in particular, was key in introducing the band to non-punk sounds such as Ronnie Hawkins, blues, R&B, Bo Diddley, Chuck Berry, and his favorite, reggae artists like Bob Marley, Peter Tosh, Toots and the Maytals, Desmond Dekker, and Burning Spear.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Nervous Recording of "Guns of Brixton"
podcast.body: Paul Simonon was reportedly very nervous about recording his lead vocal for "Guns of Brixton." This was exacerbated by an executive from the record company stopping by the studio on the day he was scheduled to cut his vocal. Simonon stared through the studio glass at the executive throughout the performance, hoping his nervousness and fear would be captured on tape. "For the entire performance Paul stared through the studio glass at the label dude Hoping that the nervousness and fear he felt about being thrust into the lead singer spotlight would translate onto tape"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Origins and Formation
podcast.body: The Clash originated from a "stillborn" group called the London SS. They officially formed in late 1976 within a severely dilapidated squat located on Davis Road in West London. Their manager was a used car salesman. "The clash evolved out of a stillborn group called the London SS."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Paul Simmonon's Musical Journey
podcast.body: Paul Simmonon initially wanted to be a painter but joined Mick Jones's new band to learn guitar. After struggling with guitar, he switched to bass at Mick's suggestion, learning on his own and becoming proficient by the band's third album. "So Mick said, alright, well then get a bass. There's two less strings. So he did, and he had to learn on his own."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Paul Simonon – Self-Taught After Failed Attempt at Guitar, Integrated Reggae into Punk
podcast.body: Paul Simonon taught himself bass after an unsuccessful initial attempt at guitar. He brought Jamaican reggae and ska sounds into The Clash's punk context, fundamentally expanding what punk bass could sound like. "Taught himself bass after trying guitar and integrated reggae and ska sounds into punk."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Paul Simonon's Early Struggles and Growth
podcast.body: When The Clash first formed, bass player Paul Simonon reportedly struggled just to play the bass. However, by the time the *London Calling* album was in production, he had taught himself how to play guitar, how to write songs, and gained significant confidence. "When the band began he struggled just to play the bass But by the time London calling went into production Paul had taught himself how to play guitar how to write songs and how to be I guess a little bit more confident"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Philosophy on Reunion (Early 2000s)
podcast.body: Following his reunion performance with Mick Jones in November 2002, Joe Strummer began publicly discussing a Clash reunion as a possibility, but emphasized it would not be a "dog and pony nostalgia show." He envisioned a proper return with a new album, new songs, and a comprehensive tour. "If the clash were ever to do it again, they'd do it right with a new album and new songs and a proper tour."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Post-Clash Career of Mick Jones
podcast.body: After being expelled from The Clash, Mick Jones formed the group Big Audio Dynamite, which went on to have a massive hit single with "E = MC²" in 1985 and 1986. This new band's success was largely due to its innovative use of sampling. "That's what became of Mick Jones after he was kicked out of the clash."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Post-Clash Reunions Attempts
podcast.body: Joe Strummer made several attempts to reform The Clash with Mick Jones over the years. The first documented attempt was in November 1985 when Joe, realizing his mistake in firing Mick, followed him on holiday to Spain to try and reconcile. However, Mick "basically laughed off the idea" because he was engaged with his own band, Big Audio Dynamite, at the time.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Post-Punk Evolution
podcast.body: After producing a couple of aggressive punk rock records, The Clash recognized the necessity to evolve musically to avoid the fate of many of their peers who dissolved after punk's initial burnout by the summer of 1979. "After a couple of fierce punk rock records, the clash knew that they had to move things forward or die like the majority of their peers."

podcast.title: Poverty and Justification for Major Label Deal
podcast.body: Prior to signing with CBS, the band was very poor, living in a rundown squat without heat and lacking money for food, to the extent of eating gig poster paste "like some kind of porridge." They justified their major label signing by arguing it was "the only way to get our music and our message out there to a worldwide audience" and claiming they would "subvert the system from within." "They were living in a rundown squat with almost no heat. They didn't even have any money for food."

podcast.body: At the time of Joe Strummer's death, his condition, intra-mural coronary artery disease, was extremely rare, with only 100 reported cases in the entire history of medicine. podcast.body: The Clash's record label was hesitant to release their records in America, reflecting the general difficulty punk music faced in gaining traction in North America due to its controversial image. "The clash's record label was afraid to put our clash records in America."

podcast.title: Reggae and Diverse Influences
podcast.body: The band was open to new ideas, particularly the reggae sounds emanating from the apartments of new immigrants in Britain. Their appreciation for reggae led them to explore ska, blues, R&B, soul, and rockabilly, incorporating these into their music. "But like the teenagers in the Slits, they were open to all kinds of new ideas, especially the new reggae sounds that were being played out of the windows of the apartments where the new immigrants lived."

podcast.title: Reggae and Ska Influence
podcast.body: Paul Simmonon absorbed deep bass sounds from New Jamaican immigrants in Britain, which were fat, warm, and groovy. These reggae and ska influences became a distinguishing feature of his rhythms as time went on. "He'd been absorbing the deep bass sounds he heard coming from the windows of New Jamaican immigrants."

podcast.body: The Clash was one of the bands Richie Edwards liked, along with Jordy Vision, The Police, The Boomtown Rats, and Blondie. "He liked Jordy Vision, the clash, the police, the Womentown rats, and blondie."

podcast.title: Ridiculous Aims

podcast.title: Terry Chimes' Career Change to Healthcare
podcast.body: After a successful music career with The Clash, Generation X, and Black Sabbath, Terry Chimes began to rethink his path in the late 1980s. Influenced by his experiences with the rock and roll lifestyle, he concluded that "the natural way of healing is far better than pumping people full of drugs." This led him to adopt a meat- and alcohol-free lifestyle, study chiropractic medicine at various schools across the UK, and learn acupuncture in China. "But by the end of the 1980s, Terry began thinking about doing something else."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: The Clash as a Voice for a Generation
podcast.body: For millions who came of age musically in the late 1970s and early 1980s, The Clash were considered "their Beatles," representing more than just punk aesthetics. They had a message and a mission rooted in integrity and honesty, serving as "the voice of a generation" that could articulate rage and alienation, and they were "their own worst critics."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Trent Reznor's View
podcast.body: The Clash were considered "cool" by Trent Reznor, but their punk rock sound was superseded in his personal inspiration by the synthesizers and drum machines employed by bands like The Human League. "Punk bands like the Sex Bistles and the Clash and the Remones were cool and everything. But the synthesizers and drum machines of the human league and OMD and Depeche mode. Now that was really cool."

podcast.title: UK Punk's Anti-Establishment Stance
podcast.body: The Clash, alongside bands like the Sex Pistols, epitomized the UK punk scene's commitment to challenging the establishment, critiquing the class system, and opposing the status quo, in contrast to the more artistic North American punk. "Bands like the Sex Pistols and the clash were all about sticking it to the establishment, kicking against the class system and railing against the status quo."

podcast.title: Undetectable Condition
podcast.body: Joe Strummer's fatal heart condition would not typically be detected through standard medical tests and would only show up during a very proper and in-depth cardiac examination. "This is something that you would never specifically test for."

podcast.body: Paul Simmonon tended to use a pick to pluck his bass strings, unlike most other bassists who used their fingers. This technique gave his Fender Precision bass a more percussive sound. "While most other bassists plucked the strings with his fingers, Paul tended to use it pick."

Their profile peaked with a 1980 show at Ontario Place in Toronto where thousands tried to get in; what followed became an infamous riot. American radio programmers loved the music but balked at the band name (for obvious reasons), prompting a temporary rename to "Teenage Heads" for US purposes. Just before a crucial US showcase in September 1980, guitarist Gord Lewis was in a serious car accident, canceling the shows and closing the window of opportunity. Original singer Frankie Venom died of throat cancer in 2008; the band continues with Dave Rave on vocals more than 40 years later. "Long after most of their original punk rock contemporaries called it quits, or died off, Teenage Head still with us."

xref.title: Move to London and Punk Scene Immersion
xref.body: In her early 20s, Hynde moved from Akron, Ohio, to London, where she deeply engaged with the burgeoning early punk scene. She contributed writing to the music magazine The NME and frequently associated with figures from bands like the Sex Pistols and The Clash while trying to form her own band. "When she was in her early 20s, she moved from Akrona, Ohio to London and immersed herself in the early punk scene. She wrote for the Music Magazine, The NME, and she hung out with people like the sex pistols in the clash, while trying to get a band off the ground."

xref.title: Multiple Stints with The Clash
xref.body: Terry Chimes was initially the drummer for The Clash in 1976 and for a period in 1977, appearing on their debut album. He was replaced by Topper Headon in mid-1977 but returned to replace Topper in 1982 and 1983 before leaving for a third time, again replaced by Topper. xref.title: Punk and Reggae Crossover
xref.body: In the 1970s, Don Letts was a DJ who played a crucial role in introducing reggae and dub music to a new generation of punk kids in clubs. At a time when punk records were scarce, Jamaican music, including dub and other Black music forms, became the foundational sound for these punks until their own genre's records emerged. "Don Letts, a confidant and friend of both the sex pistols and the clash. He was the DJ who introduced reggae and dub to a new generation of these punk kids in the 1970s in clubs where they hung out. See, there were no punk records yet, so that music, Jamaican music, dub music, black music became theirs until they had some punk records to listen to."
